brief: JPM says it no longer has a baseline model for the Iran conflict's endgame: assumed economic red lines ($100 oil, $5 gasoline, 4% inflation, a 5-handle on the 10-year yield) have all been crossed without producing an exit. Brent trades near $106 against a $90 September fair-value estimate; the $16 premium implies the market is pricing roughly 4 mbd of additional supply loss on top of the 10 mbd already disrupted, not a confirmed reduction. New pressure points this week include Houthi advances toward Bab el-Mandeb, a Saudi East-West pipeline attack, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries (one over 1,200 km inside Russia), and no de-escalation signal ahead of the September 24 Trump-Xi meeting. JPM revisits its April 'Illusion of Plenty' thesis: it expected a 1.6bn-barrel drawdown pushing prices toward $100+, but only 555mb drew, about a third of forecast, because governments leaned on demand destruction (-4.4 mbd) rather than stocks, keeping Brent's average at $94. Remaining OECD and Chinese releasable inventory, roughly 250mb, can still absorb the disruption toward a 7.65bn-barrel stress threshold, capping prices for now, though a persistent disruption would still add $7-8/bbl by 4Q26 and December.
